verified_ref: Yaksha Prashna, answer on the best of fortunes, wealth, gains and joys. BORI critical edition 3.297.52-53 (question 52, answer 53) = Ganguli, Vana Parva section CCCXI. Our chapter number 314 could not be checked against the Kumbakonam text (the digital Kumbakonam files I used stop before this part of the Vana Parva); all our other Mahabharata ids in this group match Kumbakonam numbering, so 314 is probably Kumbakonam too. The ref_label '314.75-76' is plausible as question+answer.
attribution_note: Our Sanskrit runs the Yaksha's question and Yudhishthira's answer together; speaker 'Yudhishthira' is right for the answer half only. Setting fine.
translation_note: 'dhanya' is 'what is praiseworthy / a blessing' (Ganguli: 'laudable things'), so 'best of good fortunes' is acceptable. 'dākṣya' is skill or deftness (Ganguli: 'skill'); 'competence' is fine.
context: Four Pandava brothers have drunk from a guarded lake against a voice's warning and lie dead on its bank. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's riddles first; this pair is one of a rapid series of short questions and answers. At the end he is offered one brother's life, picks Nakula over his own full brother, and the Yaksha, revealed as Dharma, revives all four.

key_terms.sense: learning, literally 'what has been heard' (sacred teaching)
contentment, being satisfied with what one has

core_teaching: Of the good things a person can have, the ones Yudhishthira ranks highest are inner or bodily rather than bought: skill, learning, health, and above all contentment.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Vana Parva CCCXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli ranks skill as the most praiseworthy thing, knowledge as the finest possession, health as the greatest gain and contentment as the highest happiness; he adds no footnote here.

The section frames every answer as tested wisdom under pressure: the brothers lie dead, and the episode closes when Yudhishthira chooses Nakula on grounds of non-injury and fairness, and all are revived.
The critical text has the same question and answer, with 'lābhānāṃ śreṣṭham ārogyam' (health the best of gains) and 'sukhānāṃ tuṣṭir uttamā'.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a gratitude check: count skill, learning, health and contentment as real wealth before measuring life by money or status.
misreadings: Not a claim that ill or less-skilled people are worse off as persons; it ranks goods, not people.
Contentment here is not giving up effort; Yudhishthira also prizes skill and learning.
cautions: Health named as 'the best gain' can sting for a reader who is chronically ill or disabled; frame it as appreciation, not a test they fail.
The scene's backdrop is four brothers lying dead; keep the riddle tone, not the deaths, in the foreground.
speaks_to: wanting to notice what is already enough
not_for: someone newly diagnosed or in chronic pain, unless framed gently
someone in acute financial hardship who may hear 'be content' as dismissal
research_note: No classical commentary consulted (Nilakantha's Bharatabhavadipa exists only as poor OCR scans I could not use). Ganguli's wording read via WebFetch summary of sacred-texts, so quotations are approximate.

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.172.20 (verified in the Kumbakonam text) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXIII (closing paragraph). BORI critical edition 12.167.21 has a different main reading (kṛtajñena sadā bhāvyaṃ mitrakāmena... mitrāt prabhavate satyaṃ mitrāt prabhavate balam); our wording matches the variant lines of BORI appendix passage *449 (lines 38-39).
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira is correct; Bhishma closes the Gautama story with it, saying he heard the story from Narada.
translation_note: Fine. 'mitrāt prabhavate sarvam' can mean 'everything comes from, or through, a friend' (Ganguli's footnote makes exactly this point about the ablative).
context: Bhishma ends the story of the ungrateful brahmin Gautama, who killed the crane Rajadharma that had fed and enriched him. In Ganguli's text the story does not end at the murder: the crane is revived by the cow Surabhi's milk-froth and nectar, and even asks Indra to bring Gautama back to life; Gautama goes home and is later cursed for his ingratitude. Bhishma then draws the moral: the ungrateful have no fame, no refuge and no expiation; be grateful and good to friends.

key_terms.sense: one who acknowledges what was done for him; grateful
a friendly disposition, the stance of a friend
arises from, or through, a friend

core_teaching: A grateful, friendly disposition is the soil of a good life; much of what we gain, materially and otherwise, comes to us from or through friends.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CLXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Bhishma closes: be grateful and work for your friends' good, since much can be gained from friends. His footnote explains that 'mitrāt' means both 'from' and 'through' a friend: friends give, or help one win, wealth and honour.
The verse sits between the sharp warning that ingratitude has no expiation (v.18-19) and the claim that gaining a friend is better than gaining wealth (v.21).

practical_reading: Read as a daily practice: notice who has helped you, say so, and treat friendship as something you invest in rather than use.
misreadings: Not a transactional 'make friends because they are useful'; the story's point is the moral horror of exploiting a benefactor.
Not a claim that people without friends are to blame for their hardship.
cautions: The source story is violent (a friend killed for food) and the surrounding verses speak of hell for the ungrateful; keep the reading on gratitude, not damnation.
speaks_to: noticing who has quietly supported you
not_for: someone who was exploited or betrayed by a 'friend' and may hear it as pressure to stay grateful to them
someone isolated and friendless, unless framed as hope
research_note: No classical commentary located. Ganguli's section number CLXXIII confirmed by reading; our data note's 'inferred' Ganguli number is correct.

verified_ref: Southern recension 4.1.121 (itihasa.io and Sanskrit Wikisource both number it 121). It is a Southern-recension-only verse, absent from the Baroda Critical Edition. Our id 4.1.101 does not match the southern numbering I could check; correct to 4.1.121.
attribution_note: Lakshmana to Rama at Lake Pampa is correct.
translation_note: 'utsāha' is better rendered 'resolute energy' or 'drive' than 'enthusiasm' (cheerfulness is not the point); the Tilaka and Shiromani gloss it as the energy that all effort rests on.
context: Arriving at Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is overwhelmed by longing for Sita: every bird and mated deer reminds him of her. Lakshmana answers the long lament by praising resolute energy, adding that energetic people do not sink in their undertakings and that by energy alone they will recover Sita; he then urges Rama to put grief behind him and remember his own great nature. Rama regains his steadiness and walks on past the lake.

key_terms.sense: resolute energy, drive, the will to undertake
hard to obtain, out of reach

core_teaching: Energy of will is the strongest resource a person has; with it, little in the world is out of reach.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Shivasahaya (Shiromani)
commentaries.gist: Both explain that every kind of effort is rooted in utsaha, so nothing is unattainable for one who has it, and by it alone the brothers will recover Sita.
On the next verses, Tilaka says Rama's nature is pure sattva, so Lakshmana's brief reminder is enough for him to drop the grief he had taken on.
Reads Rama's 'grief and delusion' theologically as compassion and tenderness, which Rama restrains so as to act within scriptural bounds.

practical_reading: Used to say that when you feel flattened, the first step back is energy itself, a small act of will, before plans or results.
misreadings: Not 'positive thinking fixes everything'; Lakshmana links energy to the concrete task of searching for Sita.
Not a rebuke of grief as weakness; Rama's grief is treated by the commentators as love, which he then channels.
cautions: The surrounding verses tell a grieving man to cast grief aside; on a Day 1 'see' slot this can feel like being told to cheer up. Pair it with the lament that precedes it.
speaks_to: starting again after a loss or setback
needing a nudge to take the first step
not_for: clinical depression where 'find your energy' may feel impossible or blaming
fresh grief in its first days
research_note: Commentary notes come only from itihasa.io's AI-generated syntheses (not yet peer-reviewed); I could not cross-check them against the commentary scans or valmikiramayan.net (bot challenge). Numbering cross-checked with Sanskrit Wikisource.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 4.7.9 in the southern text (itihasa.io) = Baroda Critical Edition 4.7.9; numbering matches.
attribution_note: Sugriva to Rama is correct; he has just shown Rama Sita's dropped ornaments and Rama has broken down.
translation_note: Fine. The three crises are glossed by the commentators as separation from a loved one, loss of wealth, and mortal danger.
context: After the fire-witnessed pact of friendship, Sugriva shows Rama the ornaments Sita dropped; Rama weeps. Sugriva, who has himself lost his wife and kingdom, says that even he, a mere monkey, does not grieve like this, asks Rama to hold back his tears, and gives this maxim. He goes on to compare the despondent person to an overloaded boat that sinks, and joins his palms begging Rama to take up his strength again.

key_terms.sense: calamity; here glossed as separation from a loved one
the steady one, possessed of fortitude
thinking it through with one's own understanding
does not sink, does not give way

core_teaching: In loss, money trouble or danger, the person who holds steady and reasons things out with his own mind does not go under.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Shivasahaya (Shiromani)
commentaries.gist: They read the three crises as separation from a dear one, loss of wealth, and life-threatening danger; reflection with one's own mind keeps the steady person afloat while the unreflecting sink like an overloaded boat.
Glosses the fortitude Rama should keep as the fixed boundary of resolute people, and Sugriva's 'ordinary monkey' as humble: if even he does not mourn to excess, Rama should not.

practical_reading: When something threatens your livelihood or safety, slow down and reason it through yourself instead of letting panic decide; that is what keeps you from sinking.
misreadings: Not 'never feel distress'; the verse is about not being swamped, and it praises thinking, not numbness.
cautions: The next verses tell Rama to restrain his tears and not grieve; avoid importing 'don't cry' into a reading for someone in pain.
speaks_to: needing a steady first step in a crisis
not_for: someone in immediate danger who needs practical help, not a maxim
fresh bereavement where 'hold steady' may feel like being told not to grieve
research_note: Commentary from itihasa.io AI syntheses only; not independently cross-checked.

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 5.136.1 (verified) = Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXVI (opening) = BORI critical edition 5.134.1. Our data's 'inferred' Ganguli number is correct.
attribution_note: Vidula to her son Sanjaya is correct, but note the nesting: Kunti tells this old story to Krishna as a message for Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Fine. 'dara' is fear, 'dīrṇa' torn or shaken.
context: Kunti, through Krishna, urges Yudhishthira to fight for his kingdom by retelling how Queen Vidula roused her son Sanjaya, who lay dejected after defeat by the king of Sindhu. In this closing speech Vidula explains why a leader must not show fear: when the king looks frightened, kingdom, army and counsellors lose heart, some defect to the enemy, and loyal friends stand by helplessly. She tells him he still has friends and hidden treasure, and he rises to win his kingdom back.
core_teaching: In a crisis a leader may be shaken inside, but should not act as a shaken person, because others take their courage or their panic from him.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Vidula says a king must not let any calamity show on him, because when the people see their king afraid, the realm, the army and the counsellors all lose heart and drift apart.

Vidula pairs the warning with encouragement: he still has friends who share his joys and sorrows, and resources he does not know of; Kunti says the story should be told to a ruler overcome by despair.
Same verse in the critical text, followed by the line that on seeing a shaken king the realm, army and ministers all fall apart.

practical_reading: For someone carrying responsibility at work or at home: you can feel fear and still choose steady actions, because the people around you take their cue from what you do.
misreadings: Not 'hide your feelings from everyone'; Vidula's own point is about the leader's conduct before those who depend on him.
Not an argument for bravado or denial.
cautions: Vidula's speeches as a whole are harsh and shaming before they turn encouraging; do not borrow their tone for a reader who already feels like a failure.
speaks_to: a parent holding steady for children
not_for: someone who needs permission to admit fear and ask for help
burnout from always having to look strong
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 169 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 4). Our id '2.163' is wrong; correct to Ayodhya 169 (doha).
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Bharat is correct. But the setting is specific: this is the end of Vasishtha's consolation on Dasharatha's death, and 'what this moment asks' is the king's funeral rites. Our prasang ('Bharat refuses the throne') belongs to a later scene (the royal council a few dohas on), not to this doha.
translation_note: Fine. Manas Piyush renders it: keep courage in your heart and do what the occasion calls for today; hearing the guru, Bharat rose and ordered all the preparations.
context: Bharat has returned to Ayodhya to find his father dead and Ram exiled, and has poured out his grief to Kausalya. Vasishtha arrives with the ministers and consoles him with teaching on the inevitability of death. This doha closes that consolation: hold firm and do today's duty. The next lines show that duty: the king's body is bathed, a bier and pyre are prepared on the Sarayu, Bharat stops the queens from following their husband into the fire, and he performs the cremation and the ten-day rites.

key_terms.sense: the occasion, what the moment calls for
the preparations, all that is needed

core_teaching: When grief is overwhelming, the guru's counsel is to steady the heart and do the duty that today requires.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (Gita Press), note on doha 169
commentaries.gist: Compares Vasishtha's 'many-sided' teaching with Valmiki and the Adhyatma Ramayana, where the sage explains that death is inevitable for the born and the self is undying, so grief should give way to the rites.
Bharat rose at once because a guru's word carries great weight; he gave orders to the ministers, and the 'what is due today' is the king's funeral.
Explains why the ministers were summoned: no one had met Bharat on his return and suspicion hung over him, so Vasishtha gathered them to clear it.

practical_reading: When everything feels unsafe, the next right task is enough: steady yourself and do what today actually requires.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving and get back to work'; the task Bharat is given is mourning itself, his father's funeral.
Not about ambition or taking the throne.
cautions: The literal 'task today' is cremating a father; avoid a light work framing that erases this, and avoid it for someone newly bereaved unless that is intended.
not_for: someone told to 'just get on with it' who needs room to feel first
research_note: Read in Manas Piyush vol. 4 (archive.org OCR), which compiles several traditional Manas commentators. Prasang assignment should be checked by the editor.

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.114.15 (verified) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXIV = BORI critical edition 12.115.14. Variant: Kumbakonam reads 'mahājane' (in a great assembly); BORI reads 'mahātmane' (about a great-souled person), and Ganguli's translation follows that sense ('proclaims the faults of a high-souled person').
attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira, answering how to respond to abuse in assemblies, is correct.
translation_note: Correct for the Kumbakonam reading. Note the alternative reading: the slanderer of a good person exposes his own faults.
context: Yudhishthira asks how a wise person should respond when a harsh, foolish man abuses him in public. Bhishma says such talk is like a crow cawing in the woods; the backbiter is like a dog, and whoever tries to answer him in kind is like a donkey sinking in ashes. The person who bears abuse in assemblies, he ends, is never hurt by words.
core_teaching: Public slander reveals the slanderer: it displays his own faults as plainly as a snake shows its raised hood.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli reads it as the evil person who broadcasts a great-souled man's faults merely advertising his own nature, like a snake spreading its hood; trying to hit back, he adds, leaves you like a donkey stuck in ash.
The verse is flanked by advice to avoid such a person entirely and not to answer back; retaliation only drags you down.

practical_reading: When someone runs you down in front of others, you do not need to win the exchange; what they say mostly shows who they are.
misreadings: Not a licence to dismiss all criticism as 'their faults'; it is about malicious public slander.
Not advice to stay silent about abuse or harassment that needs reporting.
cautions: The surrounding text uses insulting animal comparisons (dog, ass) for the slanderer; keep the reading free of contempt.
speaks_to: being belittled or passed over in public
not_for: situations of ongoing bullying or harassment where action, not endurance, is needed
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 17, chaupai lines 7-8 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 6). Our id '6.19' is wrong; correct to Lanka 17.7-8 (our 'chaupai 4' = lines 7-8 is consistent).
attribution_note: Ram to Angad, sending him as envoy to Ravana, is correct.
translation_note: Fine.
context: After the bridge is built and the army camped before Lanka, Ram consults his counsellors in the morning; Jambavan advises sending Angad. Ram blesses Angad as a store of intelligence, strength and virtue and asks him to go to Lanka on his errand. These lines are his whole briefing: he trusts Angad's judgement and asks only that he speak so the mission succeeds and Ravana's own good is served. Angad, honoured, bows and sets out.

key_terms.sense: very capable, skilled in speech and judgement

core_teaching: Speak to an adversary in a way that achieves your purpose and also serves their real good.

commentaries.gist: 'Our work' is recovering Sita; 'his good' is Ravana's safety with his family and wealth, if he yields. Calling Angad 'very capable' means he already has every quality an envoy needs.
Encouragement from elders lifts the young; by saying 'I know you are capable', Ram makes Angad capable.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing the Manas Mayank and Panjabi commentators
commentaries.gist: Offer a deeper reading: since Ram knows Ravana will not yield while alive, Ravana's true 'good' is liberation through death at Ram's hand.

practical_reading: In a hard conversation with someone who has wronged you, aim for an outcome that gets the work done without humiliating them; trust in a person's ability can itself make them rise to it.
misreadings: Not 'be nice and let them win'; Ram's purpose (Sita's return) is not negotiable.
The esoteric reading (death as Ravana's good) should not be applied to real opponents.
cautions: In the episode that follows, Ravana insults Angad and his dead father; keep the reading on how to speak, not on the confrontation.
speaks_to: preparing for a hard conversation at work
being overlooked and deciding how to speak up
not_for: someone facing an abuser, where 'consider their good' could be harmful
research_note: Read in Manas Piyush vol. 6 (archive.org OCR).

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 3.28.6 (verified) = Ganguli, Vana Parva section XXVIII = BORI critical edition 3.29.6. Our data's 'inferred' Ganguli number is correct.
attribution_note: Prahlada to his grandson Bali, quoted by Draupadi to Yudhishthira, is correct.
translation_note: Fine. 'tejas' is fiery energy, assertive might; 'force' is acceptable.
context: In the forest, Draupadi argues that Yudhishthira's endless patience with the Kauravas is wrong, and quotes Prahlada's answer to Bali. Prahlada lists the harms of always forgiving (servants and strangers disregard you, and wrongdoers grow bold) and of never forgiving (you are hated and lose friends), then gives the times for forgiveness: a past benefactor, an offence from ignorance, a first offence; a deliberate or repeated wrong should be met with firmness. Draupadi concludes it is time to act; in the next section Yudhishthira replies at length that anger destroys and forgiveness is eternal virtue.

key_terms.sense: what is truly better, the good

core_teaching: Neither force nor forgiveness is right in every case; wisdom is knowing which the situation calls for.

commentaries.gist: Prahlada says neither might nor forgiveness is always good, then lists when to pardon (a past benefactor, an error of ignorance, a first offence) and when to be firm (deliberate or repeated wrongs), weighing time, place and strength.
Yudhishthira answers Draupadi that anger is the root of ruin, that whoever does not answer anger with anger heals both parties, and that forgiveness and gentleness are eternal virtue.

practical_reading: Used to say that letting things go is not always kindness: decide each time whether this moment needs forgiveness or a firm line.
misreadings: Not a licence for revenge; Prahlada lists the harms of the never-forgiving person too.
Not a rule that you must forgive everything to be good.
cautions: Draupadi uses the verse to argue for war; the reading should stay with everyday boundaries.
Prahlada's examples include harsh punishment of servants; do not import them.
speaks_to: deciding whether to let something go
being taken for granted because you always forgive
setting boundaries after being passed over
not_for: someone wanting justification for retaliation
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 5.39.63 (verified) = Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section XXXIX = BORI critical edition 5.39.49.
attribution_note: Vidura to Dhritarashtra is correct. Setting is slightly loose: Vidura Niti takes place on the sleepless night after Sanjaya returns from the Pandavas, before he delivers Yudhishthira's message in court the next day (Ganguli, Udyoga XXXIII). 'Before the peace talks' is approximate.
translation_note: Fine. Ganguli renders ārjava as 'humble'; 'straightforward, sincere' is closer to the word.
context: Vidura is counselling the anxious, sleepless king. This verse sits in a list of people with whom Prosperity (Shri) does not stay: the grief-stricken, the idle, the uncontrolled, and the straightforward and modest person whom dull minds mistake for weak and bully. Nearby Vidura also says perseverance is the root of prosperity and that forgiveness is fitting for the strong and the weak alike.
core_teaching: Small-minded people misread straightforwardness and modesty as weakness, and try to exploit it.

commentaries.gist: Renders it as the humble and modest man being regarded as weak and persecuted by people of misdirected intelligence, in a passage about whom Prosperity avoids.

The same discourse praises perseverance as the root of prosperity and says forgiveness suits both the powerful and the weak; it describes how the world behaves rather than telling the honest to change.

practical_reading: If your honesty or modesty is being taken advantage of, the problem is the misreading, not the virtue; keep it, and add firmness.
misreadings: Not advice to stop being straightforward; it names a risk.
Not a reason to become suspicious of everyone.
cautions: As a descriptive line it can confirm a reader's bitterness; pair it with an action (a boundary) rather than leaving it as 'people are cruel'.
speaks_to: being passed over because you don't self-promote
not_for: someone already prone to seeing others as enemies
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.81.6 (verified) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXXI = BORI critical edition 12.82.6.
attribution_note: Krishna (Vasudeva) to Narada, as narrated by Bhishma to Yudhishthira, is correct.
translation_note: Meaning is right. Typo in our Sanskrit: 'दहृयं' should be 'हृदयं'.
context: Yudhishthira asks how to win over kinsmen who turn hostile; Bhishma recounts Krishna confiding in Narada. Krishna says he gives his kin half of what he has and bears their harsh words, yet those words grind his heart like a fire-stick; his clan is split between the Ahuka and Akrura factions and he cannot side with either. Narada answers that this trouble is internal and partly of Krishna's own making, and that the only weapon that works on kin is one not made of iron: sharing food, forbearance, sincerity, gentleness and due respect.

key_terms.sense: the fire-stick churned to kindle fire

core_teaching: Cruel words from one's own family keep burning long after they are spoken; even Krishna felt this.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli has Krishna's heart ground by his kinsmen's cruel words as a fire-stick is ground; his footnote explains that Ahuka and Akrura each urged Krishna to drop the other, so keeping both and losing both hurt equally.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text: Narada's reply (Ganguli, Santi LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Narada calls the trouble internal and partly self-made, and prescribes the 'weapon not made of iron': giving food, forgiveness, sincerity, mildness and honour, using soft words to turn away kinsmen's anger.

practical_reading: It names the particular sting of harsh words from family, and then (in Narada's answer) points to patience, generosity and soft speech as the way to work on such relationships.
misreadings: Not a reason to keep absorbing abuse indefinitely; Krishna asks for a remedy, and Narada also says he has partly brought the trouble on himself.
Not 'family is always toxic'.
cautions: Narada's reply partly blames Krishna; a writer should not imply the reader caused the cruelty done to them.
speaks_to: being the peacemaker in a divided family
feeling unappreciated by kin you support
not_for: someone in an abusive family situation who needs safety, not patience
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Southern recension 6.21.14-15 (itihasa.io, Sanskrit Wikisource and valmikiramayan.net all give 6.21.14 for the first line) = Baroda Critical Edition 6.14.4-5. Our id 6.21.6 is wrong; correct to 6.21.14-15. Our Sanskrit spans the end of v.14 and the start of v.15.
attribution_note: Rama to Lakshmana is correct.
translation_note: Fine: 'asāmarthyaphalāḥ' means these virtues yield, among the unworthy, only the impression of incapacity.
context: Rama has lain on darbha grass by the shore for three nights asking the Ocean for passage; the Ocean has not even appeared. Angry, his eyes reddened at the corners, Rama tells Lakshmana that gentleness is wasted on the arrogant, that the world honours the boastful man who punishes freely, and that fame and victory are not won by conciliation alone; he takes up his bow and starts to shoot. The Ocean then rises, asks for mercy and tells him Nala can build a bridge.

key_terms.sense: forbearance despite the power to punish

core_teaching: The virtues of the good (calm, forbearance, honesty, kind speech) are read as weakness by those who lack them.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Govindaraja (Bhushana)
commentaries.gist: Define the four virtues: calm as absence of anger, forbearance as pardoning offences while able to punish, straightforwardness as lack of crookedness, and kind speech; among the base these only breed the belief that the good man is weak.
Notes that Rama's eyes are reddened only at the corners, a sign of measured, controlled anger rather than rage.
Glosses the key compound as virtues that give weak results when directed toward those who have no virtues.

practical_reading: When your patience and kindness are repeatedly ignored, it may be time to add firmness; the problem is the other person's misreading, not your virtue.
misreadings: Not permission to drop kindness; Rama spent three days in patient request first.
Not an endorsement of the boastful 'punish freely' type he describes next; he is bitterly describing how the world behaves.
cautions: The verse sits in an angry speech that praises force; a reader who is hurt may hear it as license for retaliation. The episode itself ends with Rama redirecting his arrow when the Ocean responds.
speaks_to: being ignored after repeated polite requests
not_for: someone already inclined to anger or revenge
situations where the 'unworthy' party is a child or someone vulnerable
research_note: itihasa.io syntheses are AI-generated; the valmikiramayan.net page has only word glosses, no commentary, but confirms numbering and sense.

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 14.53.15 (verified; there 15 is a four-line verse) = Ganguli, Asvamedha Parva section LIII = BORI critical edition 14.52.15 plus appendix line *105. Our data's 'inferred' Ganguli number is correct.
attribution_note: Krishna to the sage Uttanka is correct, but the setting is out of order: when Krishna says this, Uttanka has only asked, hopefully, whether Krishna made peace between the cousins. Uttanka's rage and threat to curse come immediately after, in response to this answer.
translation_note: Fine. The Kumbakonam verse continues: so they all met their death with sons and kin, and destiny cannot be overcome by intellect or strength.
context: Returning to Dvaraka after the war, Krishna meets the ascetic Uttanka in the desert. Uttanka asks whether Krishna has established lasting brotherhood between the Kurus and Pandavas. Krishna says he tried hard but they would not be reconciled, so they destroyed one another, ignoring his counsel and Bhishma's and Vidura's. Uttanka, furious that Krishna did not force them to stop, threatens a curse; Krishna asks him to first hear his teaching on the self, and goes on to explain his nature and his repeated pleading with the Kauravas.
core_teaching: One can make every honest effort for peace, but cannot force others to accept it.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Krishna says he tried his utmost to bring the Kauravas to accord, failed, and so they all died; he adds that neither intellect nor strength can override what is ordained.
Later in the same reply Krishna repeats the point: in human form he pleaded with them piteously, but in their delusion they would not accept his beneficial words.

practical_reading: When a rift in the family or with a friend will not heal despite real effort, you can recognise that you did what you could; reconciliation needs both sides.
misreadings: Not 'give up after one attempt'; Krishna stresses sustained effort.
Not fatalism excusing inaction; the destiny line comes after effort.
cautions: The answer goes on to the total slaughter of both families, and Uttanka's anger at Krishna mirrors a reader's anger; acknowledge that anger rather than dismissing it.
speaks_to: guilt over a rift you could not repair
not_for: someone who has not yet tried to repair a relationship and may use it as an excuse
research_note: No classical commentary located.

core_teaching: Some troubles cannot be met alone; find an ally who shares your kind of trouble, because without that friendship success is not in sight.

commentaries.gist: Read the preceding verse through royal policy: of the six expedients, the one Rama needs is alliance (samashraya), and one touched by deep misfortune is best allied with another who shares that lot.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja and Rama Varma on 3.72.9-10

misreadings: Not 'use people'; the alliance with Sugriva becomes a real, mutual friendship.

not_for: someone who has been hurt by a friend and is not ready to trust

misreadings: Not resentment toward Dasharatha; Rama goes on willingly and without blame.
cautions: Implies the parent avoided a hard conversation; for a reader hurt by a parent, avoid turning it into an accusation.

hurt by how a decision was communicated
not_for: someone who needs to hear the other person's side first

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 15, chaupai lines 5-6 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 6; other passages in Manas Piyush cite it as 5.15). Our id '5.13' is wrong; correct to Sundar 15.5-6.
attribution_note: Ram's message to Sita delivered by Hanuman is correct.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Hanuman has dropped Ram's ring to Sita in the Ashoka grove and told her Ram's story. He now gives Ram's message: since their separation everything that once gave joy (moon, breeze, flowers, rain) has turned painful. Speaking would lighten the pain a little, but there is no one who knows it; only Ram's own mind knows the truth of their love, and that mind always stays with her. Sita weeps; Hanuman asks her to hold on, saying Ram's arrows will burn the demons like moths in fire.

key_terms.sense: the essence or truth of love

core_teaching: Speaking of pain lightens it a little, but some grief is so private that no one else can share it; the heart alone knows the love it misses.

commentaries.gist: Glosses: telling does ease grief, but whom can I tell when no one knows this pain? Only one who understands the pain can be told; so it stays inside, burning.
Suggests the hidden sense that Lakshman is with Ram, yet these words are not fit to say to him; and notes the source in the Prasanna Raghava drama.
Reads the message as a triad: Ram bears the pain in body, says nothing to anyone in speech, and keeps his mind with Sita; 'a little' because only reunion removes the whole pain.

practical_reading: It validates the loneliness of grief: telling helps, but it is hard when no one seems to understand; that is a reason to find the one person who might.
misreadings: Not a claim that talking does not help; the line says it does, a little.
cautions: In the original it is a lover's message; for a breakup or bereavement, keep focus on the loneliness, not on certainty of reunion.
not_for: someone isolated who needs to be encouraged to reach out rather than told no one understands
research_note: Read in Manas Piyush vol. 6 (archive.org OCR).

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.27.12 (verified) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII = BORI critical edition 12.28.12. Our data's Ganguli section XXVIII is correct.
attribution_note: The sage Ashma answering King Janaka, as told by Vyasa to Yudhishthira, is correct.
translation_note: Fine. Ganguli renders the pair as delusion of the mind and the onset of distress.
context: After the war Yudhishthira, burning with grief for slaughtered kin, has resolved to end his life; Vyasa consoles him with Ashma's discourse to Janaka on how to bear the coming and going of kin and wealth. Ashma says a ruler should understand the sorrows of his people in order to remedy them, and gives this two-cause analysis. He goes on at length about time and destiny bringing gain and loss, old age and death to everyone, and urges bearing both joy and sorrow without elation or collapse.

key_terms.sense: confusion or delusion of the mind

core_teaching: Mental pain has two sources, a confused mind or something unwanted happening; seeing which one you are facing is the start of healing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli names the two causes as a deluded mind and the arrival of misfortune, with no third; his note adds that the many other woes listed spring from these same two.
Ashma frames the analysis as knowledge a king needs to relieve his subjects' sorrows, then stresses that old age, death, gain and loss come to all in time's course.

practical_reading: Ask of a painful feeling: is this about what actually happened, or about how my mind is spinning around it? Each needs a different response.
misreadings: Not 'it's all in your head'; one of the two causes is a real, unwanted event.
Not dismissing grief as delusion.
cautions: The frame story is Yudhishthira resolved to end his life; do not foreground this.
The chapter leans heavily on destiny and time as the cause of all fortune, which can feel fatalistic or dismissive to fresh grief.
speaks_to: understanding why loss hurts so much
rumination after a breakup or departure
sorting what can be changed from what can't
not_for: acute suicidal distress (refer to support, not analysis)
the first days of bereavement

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.338.12 and 12.338.11 (verified; our Sanskrit gives 12 then 11) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section CCCXXXI = BORI critical edition 12.317.11-12. The same lines recur in the critical apparatus as Manu's teaching (BORI 12.198, appendix *540).
attribution_note: Narada to Shuka is correct.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Narada comes to the young Shuka and offers teachings to dispel grief. He says the man of little understanding suffers from meeting the unwanted and losing the loved; grieving for what is past only adds a second sorrow to the first; those who see the course of life clearly do not weep. Then come these lines: when pain arrives that no effort can ward off, do not keep dwelling on it. He adds that mental pain is cured by wisdom as bodily pain by medicine, and that where grief can be averted one should act on the remedy as soon as the chance appears.

key_terms.sense: should not keep dwelling on, brood over
where no effort can be made

core_teaching: For pain that nothing can fix, the medicine is to stop brooding on it; dwelling feeds it, it does not dissolve it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CCCXXXI)
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli's rendering, when an unavoidable grief arrives one should stop dwelling on it, since refusing to brood is its cure and brooding feeds it. His note on the nearby 'one sorrow becomes two' line: indulging sorrow makes it grow.
Narada pairs this with the advice that where grief can be averted, one should apply a remedy as soon as an opportunity arises, so the counsel is limited to what truly cannot be changed.
The same verses appear attributed to Manu, followed by the line that wisdom heals mental pain as medicine heals the body, showing this was a stock teaching.

practical_reading: When you have done all you can and the pain remains, gently steering attention away from rumination is a remedy, not avoidance.
misreadings: Not 'suppress your feelings'; it targets brooding, and only where nothing can be done.
Not an instruction to forget the person who left.
cautions: The same passage says the wise do not shed tears; for grief, keep the anti-rumination point and leave out the no-tears line.
speaks_to: pain one can no longer act on
not_for: early grief that needs expression
situations where something can and should still be done
research_note: No classical commentary located; Ganguli notes the commentator is silent on a nearby verse.

attribution_note: Sita's words to Ram, spoken to Hanuman as a message, are correct. This entry has no prasang in our data; it belongs with 'Hanuman reaches Sita' (Sita's token and message).
translation_note: Softens the plea. Texts differ on one word: itihasa.io reads 'mahotsāhāṃ kṛpām' (compassion full of great energy), while valmikiramayan.net glosses 'mahotsāhaḥ' (you, of great strength). Either way Sita is urging the mighty Ram to act; in context she is reproaching him for delaying to punish her abductor. 'Great-hearted kindness' loses that. Suggest: 'Mighty one, best of men, show me your compassion in action; with you as my protector, I still look like one who has none.'
context: Sita gives Hanuman a secret token for Ram: the story of the crow that attacked her, at which Ram once loosed a Brahma-weapon. Then she reproaches him: he used such a weapon for a mere crow, so why does he pardon the one who carried her off? She asks for energetic compassion, saying that though she has him as protector she seems protectorless, and reminds him that he himself taught that compassion is the highest dharma.

key_terms.sense: compassion full of great energy, active mercy

core_teaching: Sita feels abandoned despite being loved, and asks that love show itself in decisive action.

commentaries.gist: Having given a token known only to Ram, Sita adds a reproachful plea: he used the Brahma-weapon for a crow on her account, so why pardon her abductor? With him as lord, she seems lordless.

Glosses the line as Sita asking Rama, best of men and of great strength, to show her mercy: with him as protector she still looks protectorless. The previous note concerns the Brahma-missile hurled even at a crow.

practical_reading: Names the ache of feeling alone even when someone loves you, and the honest wish that their love would show up in action.
misreadings: Not a statement that she has been abandoned; she is certain of Ram's love and is urging him to act.
cautions: Its edge is reproach; for someone who has been left, it can deepen blame toward the person who left.
speaks_to: waiting for someone to come through
not_for: someone left permanently, where the hope of rescue is not real

core_teaching: 'Out of sight, out of mind' is true only of the ungrateful; real love does not fade with distance.

commentaries.gist: Sita first cites the worldly maxim that love fades when the beloved is out of sight, then at once rejects the suspicion: only the ungrateful let affection perish; grateful Ram will not.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Shivasahaya (Shiromani) on the preceding verse

practical_reading: Distance tests love but does not end it; trust the people who have shown you they are loyal.
misreadings: Not a claim that anyone who drifts away is ungrateful; it is Sita's reassurance about one proven person.
cautions: The verses just before imagine the loved one dead of grief; do not import that into a reading for someone far from parents.
speaks_to: living far from parents or family
not_for: someone who has actually been abandoned and may hear 'they would never forget you' as false

attribution_note: Bhishma to Yudhishthira is correct.
translation_note: Omits a clause: 'prāyaścittī tathā bhavet' means that if one does sleep past sunrise one should perform an expiation (Ganguli renders it so). Otherwise right.
context: Yudhishthira asks why some people die young and how one gains long life, fame and prosperity. Bhishma answers that conduct (achara) is the cause, and gives a long list of daily rules: rise before the sun, greet parents and teachers first on rising, clean the teeth, honour elders by standing and offering a seat, avoid malice. The list mixes timeless courtesies with rules of ritual purity, caste and marriage of its time.

key_terms.sense: one who must perform an expiation

core_teaching: Good conduct in small daily things, like rising early and greeting one's parents and teachers first, is what builds a long and good life.

commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Bhishma says not to lie in bed after sunrise, and to make amends if one does; the first act on rising should be to greet parents, teachers or other honoured elders, and this is what wins long life.
Bhishma's thesis is that conduct, more than learning or wealth, gives long life; he adds that old people should be greeted by standing and offering a seat, and that malice shortens life.

practical_reading: A daily act of respect, such as greeting your parents first thing (or calling them, if far away), is a small habit that shapes a good life.
misreadings: Not a literal promise that early risers live longer.
Not a demand to obey parents unconditionally, though the same chapter says so elsewhere.
cautions: The same chapter tells readers to obey parents' and teachers' commands without judging them, and includes caste and gender rules; do not import these.
For someone estranged from or grieving parents, 'greet your parents' can hurt.
speaks_to: living far from parents and wanting a daily connection
not_for: someone whose parents have died recently
someone estranged from abusive parents

translation_note: Fine. 'mā vyavarorudhaḥ' is 'do not depose or obstruct him'. Our 'line' ('let him still feel he leads') is an interpretive softening; the verse is about not displacing the king.
context: The charioteer Sumantra returns to Ayodhya and tells the grieving Dasharatha what Ram said at parting: Kausalya should drop pride and honour Kaikeyi and treat Bharata as king; Bharata, as prince regent, should serve their father on the throne and not displace the old king; and, weeping, Ram asked that Bharata look on Kausalya as his own mother. Dasharatha dies of grief soon after, so Bharata never gets to act on this.

key_terms.sense: do not depose, do not obstruct
the position of crown prince, regency

core_teaching: Ram asks his brother to rule only as the old father's agent, honouring him rather than pushing him aside.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Govindaraja (Bhushana)
commentaries.gist: Gloss the key verb as 'do not depose him from the throne' (Tilaka) or 'do not obstruct him' (Bhushana); Bharata should serve as prince regent while their aged father reigns.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhushana on the preceding verses
commentaries.gist: Explain Ram's advice to Kausalya to drop pride of rank and jealousy toward co-wives, and that a king is senior by office, not years, so even his mother should honour Bharata as king.

practical_reading: As parents age, help them without taking over; let them keep their dignity and say in their own life.
misreadings: Not 'never make decisions for an ageing parent' where safety requires it.
cautions: Dramatic irony: the father dies of grief soon after; avoid pairing with a reader whose parent is dying unless intended.
speaks_to: caring for ageing parents from a distance
not_for: someone whose parent is controlling or abusive

a father is higher than the sky
the mind is swifter than wind

core_teaching: Parents carry a weight and height beyond measure, while the mind outruns the wind and worries outnumber the grass.

commentaries.gist: Tilaka reconstructs the day: Rama had spent three watches taking leave and giving away his wealth, so 'now' points to the night about to fall; both gloss the last word as 'you will depart at dawn'.

missing family meals and time together
not_for: someone whose parent died while they were away (could intensify guilt)

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.81.11 (verified) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXXI = BORI critical edition 12.82.11.
attribution_note: Krishna to Narada, narrated by Bhishma, is correct.
translation_note: Our translation reverses the sense. The Kumbakonam line 'naikasya jayam āśaṃse dvitīyasya parājayam' means 'I wish neither for the victory of one nor for the defeat of the other'; the BORI text reads 'I wish for victory to one and no defeat to the other', and Ganguli renders 'invoking victory to both'. Krishna is not saying cheering one means wishing the other's defeat; he is saying, like the gamblers' mother, he cannot want either to lose. Suggested: 'I am like the mother of two gamblers playing against each other: I can wish neither one's win nor the other's loss.'
context: Krishna tells Narada his clan is split between the Ahuka and Akrura factions; each urges him to drop the other, and both having and not having them is painful. He compares himself to the mother of two gamblers playing each other and asks what would be good for himself and his kin. Narada prescribes the 'weapon not of iron': sharing, forbearance, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
core_teaching: When two people you love are pitted against each other, you cannot root for either one's defeat; that is the torn position of the peacemaker.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Krishna is like the mother of two brothers gambling against each other who prays that both may win; the footnote on the Ahuka-Akrura rivalry explains why he needs both sides.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text: Narada's counsel (Ganguli, Santi LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Advises winning kin with food shared, forgiveness, sincerity, mildness and honour, and soft words that turn away anger.

practical_reading: For a parent between two quarrelling children (or a friend between two friends), it names the ache of loving both and wanting neither to lose; Narada's answer points to patience and gentle speech.
misreadings: Not advice to stay neutral at all costs where one party is harming the other.
cautions: Fix the translation before use: as written it suggests taking sides is unavoidable, which is the opposite of the image.
not_for: situations of abuse between family members, where neutrality is harmful
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 7-8 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 5; also cross-cited there as 4.14). Our id '4.15' is wrong; correct to Kishkindha 14.7-8.
attribution_note: Ram to Lakshman, describing the monsoon on Mount Pravarshana, is correct.
translation_note: Fine. 'samiṭi samiṭi' is 'gathering, collecting from all around'; 'bit by bit' is a fair rendering.
context: Waiting out the rainy season with Lakshman on Mount Pravarshana, Ram reads every sight of the monsoon as a lesson. Just before, he compares muddy rainwater to the soul clouded by maya; here water gathering into ponds is like virtues coming to a good person, and river water reaching the ocean becomes still like a soul that has found Hari. The description continues into autumn.

key_terms.sense: gathering bit by bit from all around

core_teaching: Good qualities collect in a good person gradually, the way water gathers into a pond; and the soul becomes still on reaching God as a river does in the sea.

commentaries.gist: Virtues enter the good person's heart gradually, not all at once, and they come of themselves, as water flows into a pond without the pond striving.

The rain falls drop by drop and the ponds fill; so a good person becomes an ocean of virtue by gathering one or two qualities at a time from others, like Dattatreya learning from twenty-four teachers.
Wherever rain falls it collects in the pond, its proper vessel; so whoever speaks of a virtue, it goes to the good person who can hold it.

practical_reading: Growth comes in small amounts that add up; you do not need to become good, or capable, all at once.
misreadings: Not 'virtue comes without any effort' as an excuse for inaction (one commentator stresses effortlessness; another stresses gathering).
Not a claim that people without visible virtues are bad.
cautions: Pandit Ramkumar's 'effortless' reading slightly cuts against using it to motivate effort; the 'drop by drop' reading (Karunasindhu) suits a can't-get-started plan better.
not_for: someone needing urgent decisive action

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.178.26 (verified) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXX = BORI critical edition 12.173.25.
attribution_note: Indra in the form of a jackal speaking to the young brahmin Kashyapa, as told by Bhishma, is correct.
translation_note: Fine. Ganguli's footnote: even copious draughts do not slake thirst permanently; it returns.
context: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that wisdom is the best refuge, through the story of Kashyapa: knocked down by a proud rich merchant's chariot, the young brahmin resolves to die, saying a poor man has no use for life. A jackal (Indra in disguise) tells him how fortunate he is to have hands and a human birth, says taking one's life is sinful, and explains that no condition brings contentment: the rich want kingship, kings want godhood, gods want Indra's throne. Then comes this verse on craving that grows with each gain.

key_terms.sense: fuel sticks fed to a fire

core_teaching: Getting what you want does not satisfy craving; like fire fed with fuel, it only blazes higher.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CLXXX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's jackal says getting what we want never brings contentment; thirst returns however much water there is, and the urge to acquire flares with each gain like fire with fresh fuel. His note: quenched thirst always returns.
The jackal lists the endless ladder of wanting (wealth, kingship, godhood, Indra's seat) and then reminds Kashyapa that both joy and sorrow are already in him, so why lament.

practical_reading: If each thing you get only sharpens the wanting, the answer is not one more thing; notice the fire before feeding it.
misreadings: Not a rule against ever wanting or earning anything.
Not contempt for the poor.
cautions: The frame story is a young man resolved to die after humiliation; do not foreground it.
The jackal's argument includes caste-ranking of births (brahmin as highest); leave it out.
speaks_to: chasing the next purchase or promotion
not_for: someone in real poverty, who may hear it as 'stop wanting basics'
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 12.176.25 (verified) = Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXVII = BORI critical edition 12.171.25.
attribution_note: Manki addressing Desire (Kama), as told by Bhishma, is correct.
translation_note: Fine. 'saṃkalpa' is the mind's forming of an intention or fancy; Ganguli translates 'Will' and discusses the term in a footnote.
context: Yudhishthira asks what a man should do when thirst for wealth overwhelms him and he cannot get it. Bhishma tells of Manki, who after repeated failures spent his last money on two young bulls; a startled camel ran off with both dangling from its neck. Watching them carried to their death, Manki sees through desire and sings to it: you have made me your toy; I know your root, you are born of my own resolving, and I will stop resolving you. He ends by choosing tranquillity.

key_terms.sense: mental intention, the fancy that forms a want

core_teaching: Desire grows from our own mental fixing on things; stop feeding that fixation and desire withers at the root.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CLXXVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli takes saṃkalpa as 'Will': desire springs from it, so giving it up destroys desire at the root. His footnote muses that if kama means a formed desire for specific objects, resolve can indeed be called its base.

Manki adds that wealth gives anxiety when gained and grief like death when lost; he resolves to bear insults and seek happiness within, and Bhishma presents him as a model of one freed from attachment.

practical_reading: Catch the moment a want is being built up in your mind, the planning and picturing, and stop feeding it; that is where desire gets its strength.
misreadings: Not a demand to give up all goals; Manki's insight is about compulsive craving that keeps hurting him.
Not self-blame for loss.
cautions: Manki's song comes out of loss and despair; for a reader who has just lost money or a job, keep the tone gentle, not 'you brought it on yourself'.
speaks_to: letting go after a financial loss
not_for: someone in fresh financial crisis who needs practical help first
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 149, chaupai lines 5-6 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 2). Our id '1.141' is wrong; correct to Bal 149.5-6.
attribution_note: Listener is wrong. In the Manas, Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva had come to Manu many times and he did not ask them for anything; the one who now stands before Manu and Shatarupa and offers the boon is the Supreme Lord in his own form (Ram, with Sita), as Manas Piyush notes. Change listener from 'Vishnu' to 'the Supreme Lord (Ram)'.
translation_note: Fine.
context: King Manu and Queen Shatarupa, after long austerity, see the Lord appear and are told to ask any boon. Manu says that seeing the Lord's feet fulfils every wish, yet one great longing remains, which feels too much to ask because of his own smallness: like a pauper before the wishing tree who hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power. The Lord tells him to drop the hesitation, since nothing is withheld from him; Manu then asks for a son like the Lord himself.

key_terms.sense: the wish-fulfilling tree of the gods
hesitates out of shyness or unworthiness

core_teaching: We hesitate to ask for what we truly want because we feel too small for it, not knowing how generous the giver is.

commentaries.gist: Manu casts himself as the pauper and the Lord as the wishing tree whose power he does not grasp, so he shrinks from asking. The 'great wealth' he wants is the Lord's lifelong presence as a son.
Sees here the attitude of 'karpanya' surrender: however much one has practised, one should never think 'I have done something'; humility and love, not years of austerity, win the Lord.
The poverty here is ignorance: the deluded person assumes the highest joy is not for him, so he does not even ask for it.

practical_reading: Feeling 'not good enough' can stop us asking for what we really want; the verse invites naming the wish anyway, trusting the giver's generosity.
misreadings: Not 'ask God for wealth'; the 'much' Manu wants is the Lord's lasting presence.
cautions: Devotional framing; for a non-devotional reader, keep the point about hesitating to ask.
speaks_to: feeling unworthy of what you want
hesitating to ask for help or a raise
not_for: someone whose request has already been refused painfully

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 3.32.58 (verified) = Ganguli, Vana Parva section XXXII = BORI critical edition 3.33.54.
attribution_note: Draupadi to Yudhishthira is correct. She says she learned these teachings, which go back to Brihaspati, from a learned brahmin her father kept, who recited them to her when she sat on her father's lap.
translation_note: Fine. BORI ends the line with 'bhārata' (O Bharata) where our text has 'śobhanā' (fine prosperity); the meaning is unchanged.
context: Draupadi, still pressing Yudhishthira to act, argues that every creature must act, that those who trust only fate or chance are the worst of men, and that success depends on effort combined with circumstances, so one should not despair at failure. Immediately before this line she says a person should seek out the weak points of enemies; immediately after, that success depends on acting according to time and circumstance. She closes by naming her source: Brihaspati's teachings as recited by a learned brahmin at her father's house.

key_terms.sense: one who looks down on himself

core_teaching: Never look down on yourself; one who despises himself cannot flourish.

commentaries.gist: Renders: no man should ever disparage himself, for the man who disparages himself never earns high prosperity; success depends on acting according to time and circumstances.
Draupadi also says no one should despair at failure, since success needs several conditions besides exertion, but without exertion there is none; confident, active people succeed.

practical_reading: Self-contempt is not humility; it drains the energy you need to act. Treat yourself as someone worth effort.
misreadings: Not arrogance or self-promotion.
Not 'confidence guarantees success'; Draupadi says success depends on many factors.
cautions: The line sits in a speech that also advises searching out enemies' weaknesses and wishing them ill; keep it on self-respect.
speaks_to: low confidence before a new effort
not_for: someone in a depressive episode who may hear 'don't despise yourself' as one more thing they are failing at, unless framed gently
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Southern recension 6.22.51 (itihasa.io); Sanskrit Wikisource numbers it 6.22.53. First line southern-only; second line = Baroda Critical Edition 6.15.13. Our id 6.22.42 matches neither; correct to 6.22.51 (note variant 53).
attribution_note: Nala to Rama is correct. Note it is the Ocean who first names Nala as able to build the bridge; Nala then confirms it.
translation_note: Fine.
context: When Rama's anger finally brings the Ocean before him, the Ocean asks him to spare it and says the monkey Nala, son of the divine architect Vishvakarma, can build a bridge. Nala steps forward: his mother was granted a boon that she would bear a son equal to Vishvakarma; the Ocean has reminded him of it, and he would not have praised his own abilities unasked. Then this verse: I can build it, let the monkeys start today. Hundreds of thousands of monkeys rush to the forest to haul trees and rocks.
core_teaching: Once reminded of an ability he had kept quiet about, Nala owns it plainly and calls for work to start that very day.

commentaries.gist: Explains Nala's earlier silence: he had forgotten his gift until the Ocean reminded him, and boasting unasked at the start of a task inspires little trust.
Attributes Nala's prior silence to modesty, embarrassment at self-praise.
Reads 'let them build' as Nala telling the monkeys to gather materials under his direction.

practical_reading: You may have abilities you have stopped noticing; when someone names them, say yes plainly and begin today.
misreadings: Not boasting; the commentators stress Nala's modesty.
Not 'do it all alone'; the whole army builds.
not_for: someone pressured to overcommit

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand doha 10, chaupai lines 5-8 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 5). Our id '3.7' is wrong; correct to Aranya 10.5-8 (our 'chaupai 3' begins correctly at line 5).
attribution_note: Sutikshna speaking to himself is correct; Manas Piyush (Pa. Pa. Pra.) calls the passage a soliloquy.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Sutikshna, a disciple of Agastya devoted to Ram in thought, word and deed, hears that Ram is coming and runs out. On the way he wonders whether the friend of the lowly will really show grace to someone as worthless as himself, listing all he lacks; then he remembers Ram's one habit, that whoever has no other refuge is dear to him, and rejoices that his eyes will see Ram today. Lost in love he forgets the way, dances and turns back; Ram watches hidden behind a tree, then wakes him and embraces him.
core_teaching: Grace does not depend on our qualifications: the one who has nowhere else to go is the one God loves.

commentaries.gist: 'One habit' shows that meeting Ram is caused by his compassion, not by spiritual practices; Sutikshna relies not on any practice but on having no other support, as Atri and Sharabhanga also confessed lacking all means.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pa. Pa. Pra. (Swami Prajnananand)
commentaries.gist: Taking two sayings of Ram together, concludes that 'having no other refuge' is itself a complete form of devotion needing no other means: very simple, yet very hard to attain.
The grace Sutikshna hopes for is to be embraced as Ram's own servant, and the 'own servant' is defined as one who has no other hope.

practical_reading: When you feel you have nothing to show, the verse says that very emptiness, honestly owned, is enough to be loved.
misreadings: Not 'effort and practice don't matter'; Sutikshna is described as devoted in thought, word and deed.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
cautions: Strongly devotional; frame for non-devotional readers as being accepted without having to earn it.
not_for: someone who uses self-deprecation to avoid change

verified_ref: BORI critical edition 3.280.6 = Ganguli, Vana Parva section CCXCIV (wisdomlib labels it 'CCLXLIV'). Our chapter number 297 could not be checked in the Kumbakonam files available (see mbh.3.314.75).
attribution_note: Savitri to her father-in-law Dyumatsena is correct.
translation_note: Fine. Typo in our Sanskrit: 'व्यसंसायकृतं' should be 'व्यवसायकृतं'. Ganguli renders vyavasāya as 'perseverance', the cause of a vow's success.
context: Savitri knows, from Narada's prophecy, that her husband Satyavan will die on a set day. Four days before it she begins a severe three-night vow, standing without food. Her blind father-in-law, the exiled king Dyumatsena, is distressed at its harshness; she reassures him with this verse, and he replies that he cannot ask her to break it. On the fated day she goes into the forest with Satyavan, and later wins his life back from Yama.

key_terms.sense: the cause, what carries it through

core_teaching: A resolve begun with determination is carried through by that same determination.

commentaries.gist: In Ganguli, Savitri asks her father-in-law not to grieve: she began the vow with steady resolve, and such resolve is what brings a vow to completion; he says he cannot ask her to give it up.
Dyumatsena calls the three-night observance extremely severe; Savitri answers with this verse; he replies he is unable to say 'break your vow'.

practical_reading: When others worry you have taken on too much, your own steady resolve is both the reason you started and the thing that will carry you through.
misreadings: Not a case for ignoring health in extreme fasting or vows.
Not 'willpower conquers death'; Savitri's victory comes through wisdom and Yama's boons.
cautions: Background is foreknowledge of a husband's death; avoid for a reader facing a partner's terminal illness unless intended.
not_for: someone in an unhealthy restriction pattern (fasting, overwork)
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 5.12.10 in the southern text (itihasa.io, Sanskrit Wikisource) = Baroda Critical Edition 5.10.10; numbering matches.
attribution_note: Hanuman to himself is correct.
translation_note: Fine. 'anirveda' is freedom from despondency, undaunted persistence.
context: Hanuman has searched Ravana's palace, inner apartments and much of Lanka without finding Sita. He dreads facing Jambavan, Angad and the waiting monkeys empty-handed and even thinks he might fast to death. Then he rallies: freedom from despondency is the root of success and the highest happiness; he will search again where he has not looked. He goes on to search the remaining places and later finds Sita in the Ashoka grove.
core_teaching: Refusing to lose heart is the root of success and itself the highest happiness; so search again where you have not yet looked.

commentaries.gist: After a moment of despondency Hanuman embraces anirveda, which Tilaka defines as the buoyant readiness of the faculties to act; the effort it produces brings enthusiasm and steadiness of mind.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja (Bhushana) and Shivasahaya (Shiromani)
commentaries.gist: Read the next verse's effort as effort prompted by persistence; Govindaraja reads the preceding fasting-unto-death line as referring to the waiting monkeys rather than Hanuman himself.
Renders freedom from despondency as the root of prosperity and the greatest comfort, adding that it drives success in all undertakings.

practical_reading: When an effort fails, the next step is not giving up but looking again in the places you skipped.
misreadings: Not 'never rest'; it is about not giving way to despair.
cautions: The verses just before mention Hanuman considering fasting to death; do not foreground that.
not_for: someone who needs to stop and rest rather than push on
research_note: itihasa.io syntheses AI-generated; valmikiramayan.net confirms sense but has no commentary on this verse.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 79, chaupai lines 5-6 per Manas Piyush (vol. 6; its page headings read 'doha 79 (5)' and vol. 2 cross-cites it as 6.79). Our id matches this numbering. Caution: some editions place this passage before doha 80, so it may also be cited as Lanka 80.
attribution_note: Ram to Vibhishan is correct.
translation_note: Fine. 'sīla' is glossed in Manas Piyush as pure conduct or good character.
context: Ravana rides out on a chariot while Ram stands on foot; Vibhishan, out of love, grows anxious and asks how Ram can win without a chariot or armour. Ram answers that the chariot that brings victory is a different one, and describes a chariot made of dharma: courage and fortitude its wheels, truth and character its flag, strength, discernment, self-control and kindness its horses, yoked with forgiveness, compassion and equanimity. Whoever has such a chariot, he ends, can conquer even the great enemy, worldly existence itself.

key_terms.sense: valour, courage to enter the fight

core_teaching: Real victory rides on inner qualities: courage and steadiness as wheels, truth and character as flag, and self-mastery and kindness as horses.

commentaries.gist: Links valour and fortitude to the Gita's list of a warrior's natural qualities (18.43) and to the maxim of courage against enemies and patience in adversity; glosses sila as pure conduct.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, note citing Ramanuja's Gita commentary
commentaries.gist: Defines valour as the capacity to enter battle without fear, and fortitude as the capacity to finish what one has begun even when obstacles arise.
Battle chariots had two wheels; courage and fortitude are the base of the dharma-chariot, and dharma without them is lame and cannot carry anyone through.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing the Bandan Pathak commentary
commentaries.gist: Calls this passage the Manas's own battlefield Gita: as Krishna taught Arjuna, Ram teaches Vibhishan the chariot that wins over the unconquerable enemy, worldly existence.

practical_reading: When outer resources look thin compared to the opposition, build the inner chariot: courage to start, patience to continue, truthfulness, and self-control.
misreadings: Not 'resources don't matter'; it is about what ultimately decides the outcome.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 1-2 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 6). Our id '5.6' is wrong; correct to Sundar 7.1-2.
attribution_note: Vibhishan to Hanuman is correct.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Searching Lanka, Hanuman finds a house marked with Ram's name and tulsi plants; its owner Vibhishan wakes chanting Ram's name. They meet, both moved, and Hanuman tells Ram's story. Unasked, Vibhishan describes his life: he lives among the demons like the poor tongue among the teeth, and wonders whether Ram will ever show grace to one so unsupported. Hanuman reassures him that Ram loves even a lowly, restless monkey like himself.

key_terms.sense: way of living, how one gets by

core_teaching: Living among hostile people is like being the tongue among the teeth: always careful, never safe.

commentaries.gist: Having found good company, Vibhishan pours out the pain of bad company without being asked; he says 'our' to include his family; the teeth stand for death-like cruelty, a living hell.
Either the tongue is helpless, shut in with no remedy, or it gets by only through great care, since one slip and it is bitten.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar (third note)
commentaries.gist: The tongue did not choose the teeth, as Vibhishan did not choose his birth; and as the tongue remains when the teeth are pulled, he will remain when the demons are gone.
Tulsidas's similes come from everyday experience, which is why so many of his lines became proverbs.

practical_reading: It gives words to living or working among people who hurt you: constant care, no rest; and the next lines hold out hope of finding an ally.
misreadings: Not advice to stay in such a situation indefinitely; Vibhishan later leaves Lanka for Ram.
cautions: For someone in an abusive home, pair naming the situation with signposting toward safety and support.
speaks_to: living with someone who hurts you
not_for: someone in immediate danger who needs practical help first

verified_ref: Kumbakonam 5.36.37 (verified) = Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section XXXVI = BORI critical edition 5.36.35.
attribution_note: Vidura to Dhritarashtra is correct, in Vidura's own words: the Atreya-Sadhyas dialogue named in our prasang ends at v.21; this verse comes later, after Dhritarashtra asks about great families.
translation_note: Fine.
context: Vidura is counselling the sleepless king. After retelling the sage Atreya's teaching to the Sadhyas on not returning insult, he answers Dhritarashtra's question about what makes a family great: good conduct rather than wealth. Then he turns to friendship: one whose anger you fear, or whom you must serve warily, is no friend; a true friend is one you can trust like a father. He adds that a well-wisher, even unrelated, is a real kinsman and refuge.

key_terms.sense: to be approached with suspicion, warily
one would trust as in a father

core_teaching: A true friend is someone you can trust like a parent; if you fear their anger or must tiptoe around them, it is only an acquaintance.

commentaries.gist: In Ganguli's version, someone whose temper you dread, or whom you must serve nervously, is not a friend; the real friend is one you can rely on as on a father, and other ties are friendships in name only.
The next verse adds that even someone unrelated who behaves as a friend is a true kinsman, refuge and protector; the passage goes on to warn against fickle, ungrateful friends.

practical_reading: If you are always bracing for someone's temper, that is a sign the relationship is not the friendship it claims to be.
misreadings: Not 'cut off anyone who is ever angry'.
cautions: For a reader being hurt by someone close, this may prompt hard conclusions; pair with support.
not_for: someone without safe alternatives who may feel more trapped by the realisation
research_note: No classical commentary located.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 46, chaupai lines 5-6 in the Gita Press numbering used by Manas Piyush (vol. 6). Our id '5.44' is wrong; correct to Sundar 46.5-6.
attribution_note: Ram to Vibhishan is correct.
translation_note: Close. Ram first asks how Vibhishan's dharma was kept up living among the wicked, then answers himself that he knows his ways. Our 'line' ('I know how you kept your goodness') merges the question and answer; acceptable.
context: Thrown out of Lanka for advising Ravana to return Sita, Vibhishan crosses to Ram's camp; over Sugriva's suspicion Ram receives him, embraces him and seats him close. Ram greets him as 'lord of Lanka', asks after his family's welfare given his bad place of dwelling, then these lines: how did you keep your dharma living day and night among the wicked? I know your ways: wise in right conduct, with no taste for wrong. He adds that it is better to live in hell than to be given the company of the wicked. Vibhishan replies that seeing Ram's feet he is now well.
core_teaching: Ram recognises that keeping one's goodness among cruel people is hard, and affirms that Vibhishan has done it.

commentaries.gist: Welfare here means keeping dharma; a place full of the wicked is a bad home however rich, with no respite. 'I know your ways' shows their faults never stuck to him, like a jewel in a snake's hood.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pa. Pa. Pra. (Swami Prajnananand)
commentaries.gist: Such a place is unfit for practising dharma.
Reads 'friend' as also asking how Vibhishan kept up his friendship with Ram while living there.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, note on the next line
commentaries.gist: On 'better hell than wicked company', cites a Garuda Purana verse: hell exhausts sin, but evil company only increases it.

practical_reading: If you live or work among people who are cruel, it is an achievement just to stay decent; you are seen.
misreadings: Not 'stay among the wicked to prove your goodness'; the next line says better hell than such company, and Vibhishan has left.
cautions: The next line ('better hell than bad company') can feel like blame for someone who cannot leave.
speaks_to: someone being hurt by those around them
staying decent in a toxic workplace or family
not_for: someone who cannot leave and may hear 'you should have left'
